title: Earth's Frozen Regions Have Crossed Safe Limits, a Science Study Finds
dek: A Science paper led by Stockholm Resilience Centre researchers says land ice, sea ice, snow cover and permafrost have moved beyond their safe operating space, and it was published as COP31 talks continue in Antalya.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Arctic sea ice pack photographed from an aircraft

keyPoints: Researchers led by Bo Su of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Beijing Normal University say land ice, sea ice, snow cover and permafrost have crossed safe levels.
The paper was published in Science with a date of Nov. 12, 2026; the Stockholm Resilience Centre says more than 30 scientists contributed, including co-founder Johan Rockström.
The centre says these frozen landscapes were relatively stable through more than 10,000 years of Holocene conditions before climate change pushed them past their safe operating space.
The authors describe an accelerating and partly irreversible decline, driven and amplified by positive feedbacks.
The researchers say the breakdown could accelerate warming and sea-level rise and raise the risk of catastrophic floods and droughts.
body:
## What the study measured

The paper, titled "The Cryosphere Beyond a Planetary Safe Operating Space," assesses four parts of the frozen Earth system: land ice, including committed future loss; sea ice; snow cover; and permafrost. The lead author is Bo Su of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Beijing Normal University. The team includes researchers from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, Tsinghua University and other institutions, and the centre says co-founder Johan Rockström is a co-author.

The safe-operating-space framework sets precautionary limits for planetary systems. The paper defines precautionary boundaries for the planet's frozen areas, the centre says.

## Why the authors say it matters

Ice, snow and permafrost help regulate the planet's energy, water, carbon and methane cycles, the centre says. Their breakdown can accelerate warming, add to sea-level rise, degrade ecosystems and make catastrophic floods and droughts more likely. The researchers say the exposure is greatest in polar, high-mountain, coastal and low-lying regions.

## A feedback problem

The paper describes a decline that is accelerating and in part irreversible, and that is driven and amplified by positive feedbacks. In simple terms, a feedback is a loop in which warming exposes darker ground or water that absorbs more heat, which causes further warming.

## Timing at COP31

The centre said the study was published at COP31 in Antalya and called for urgent international action. Negotiators are working through their first week of talks on fossil fuels, finance and the 1.5C goal. The study gives them a new scientific reference point, though it does not by itself change any negotiating text. Our [COP31 story](/article/cop31-antalya-talks-stall-over-fossil-fuels-week-one) covers those talks.

## What we could not verify

The full paper sits behind a publisher block: our fetch of the Science article returned HTTP 403. This story therefore relies on the Stockholm Resilience Centre's research story, a Phys.org repost of that release, the PubMed record for the publication date, and the centre's publications page. We have not independently reviewed the paper's data or methods.
